description: a browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players pick a mission, spacecraft, instruments, launch vehicle and orbit, then balance mass, power, budget, data and communications before simulating the mission and getting a report on why it succeeded or failed. Skills: web development, game design, JavaScript. Not recruiting right now, as the build is already underway
summary:
Mission Architect is an interactive browser game where players design, launch and manage a space mission to Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars. Players choose a spacecraft, solar panels, battery, antenna, scientific instruments, launch vehicle and orbit while a live dashboard tracks six limits: mass, power, budget, data, communications and mission lifetime. A 2D simulation then flies the mission through its phases, including eclipse periods and, on Hard mode, random space-weather events and equipment faults. A debrief scores the result, explains why the mission succeeded or failed and how to improve, and points to similar real missions such as Landsat 9, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and MAVEN.

The challenge asks for a game that shows how mission design involves trade-offs under limited resources. Mission Architect makes that hands-on: every choice affects another resource, and there is no single perfect design. It offers Easy, Normal and Hard levels, a Sandbox mode, and a pass-the-device Team mode for two to four players with different roles who must agree before launch. Built with plain HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas 2D and Web Audio, it runs in any browser with no install. It is a simplified educational model with illustrative numbers, informed by NASA mission design resources.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

Mission Architect is an interactive, browser-based aerospace design and flight operations game where players step into the role of flight directors to configure, validate, launch, and operate scientific space missions to Earth orbit, the Moon, or Mars.

The gameplay loop operates in four interconnected stages:

  1. Target Reconnaissance & Mission Selection: Players choose an operational destination—monitoring Earth's climate and agriculture, prospecting lunar polar volatile ice, or investigating Martian atmospheric loss. Players select from Standard (Easy), Nominal (Normal), High-Stress (Hard), or Sandbox modes.
    • Chassis Bus: CubeSat, SmallSat, or Dedicated Probe bus with specific dry mass, volume constraints, and thermal tolerance.
    • Power & Communications: Solar panel surface arrays, rechargeable battery storage banks, and RF antennas (Omni, Medium-Gain, or High-Gain Cassegrain dishes).
    • Scientific Instruments: Destination-specific sensor suites (visible cameras, thermal infrared imagers, synthetic aperture radar, magnetometers, and mass spectrometers).
    • Launch Vehicle & Trajectory: Light, Medium, or Heavy-Lift rockets paired with target orbital regimes (Low Earth Orbit, Sun-Synchronous Orbit, Lunar Polar, or Areocentric Low Mars Orbit).
    • Redundant Flight Extras: Radiation-hardened electronics, cold-gas reaction thrusters, star trackers, and thermal control louvers.
  2. Live Telemetry Constraints Dashboard: A real-time telemetry console continuously tracks six interdependent aerospace resources: Mass (wet mass vs. rocket lift capacity), Power (solar irradiance generation at 1.00–1.52 AU vs. subsystem draw during daylight and eclipse battery discharge), Budget (subsystem capital cost vs. mission cap), Data Generation (sensor daily bits), Communications (RF ground station contact window and downlink bandwidth), and Expected Mission Lifetime.
  3. 2D Orbital Simulation & Anomaly Handling: Once the Flight Readiness Review reports "GO", a 5-phase orbital physics simulation runs across Launch, Transit / Insertion, Commissioning, Science Ops, and End of Mission. In Hard mode, random space weather events (solar particle events, micrometeorite strikes, reaction wheel desaturation faults) challenge the spacecraft's built-in redundancies.
  4. Post-Flight Evaluation & Debriefing: Missions receive an algorithmic score out of 100 broken down into Mission Objectives (40 pts), Science Return (25 pts), Cost & Mass Efficiency (20 pts), and Subsystem Reliability (15 pts), with a letter grade (S, A, B, C, or Fail) and transparent diagnostics explaining why the mission succeeded or where engineering trade-offs failed.

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Demystifies Systems Engineering: Rather than treating rocket science as pure propulsion, the game teaches systems trade-offs. Players quickly learn that adding powerful instruments increases data rates and power draw, requiring larger solar panels and batteries, which increases mass, necessitating a larger, more expensive rocket that may exceed the mission budget cap.
  • Lowers the Barrier to STEM Exploration: Requires zero installation, account creation, or prior aerospace background. Complex orbital mechanics, link budgets, and power balances are translated into intuitive gauges, visual status indicators, and clear feedback loops.
  • Encourages Critical Thinking over Memorization: With four difficulty settings and an unrestricted Sandbox mode, students and enthusiasts can freely experiment, observe failure modes safely, and iterate toward optimized architectures.
  • Cross-Flight Learning: The built-in flight log compares the telemetry and scores of the player's last three flights side-by-side, encouraging incremental engineering improvements.

3. Intended Impact

  • Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers: By translating authentic mission planning concepts used by mission design centers into an engaging educational game, Mission Architect bridges the gap between passive curiosity and active systems thinking for students worldwide.
  • Classroom and Workshop Collaboration: Through its pass-the-device Team Mode, educators and workshop leaders can divide classrooms into flight crews of 2 to 4 students (Mission Planner, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, Telemetry/Comms Lead), fostering genuine collaboration, communication, and consensus-building without requiring individual computers or network setup.
  • Global Accessibility: Engineered to run smoothly on low-power devices, Chromebooks, tablets, and smartphones over slow internet connections, ensuring students from any socioeconomic background can engage with aerospace principles.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Core Stack: Plain HTML5, CSS3 (custom responsive design system using CSS Custom Properties and retro console UI tokens), and Vanilla JavaScript (modern ES6+ modular architecture).
  • Rendering & Visuals: HTML5 Canvas 2D for real-time orbital timeline rendering, starry background animations, telemetry sparklines, and mission performance radar charts. Hand-crafted, responsive SVG vector graphics for destination dossiers and hardware schematics.
  • Audio Synthesis: Procedural browser sound engine built entirely with the native Web Audio API (custom oscillators, biquad filters, and gain nodes generating authentic retro mission control beeps and thruster pulses—zero external audio MP3/WAV assets).
  • No Frameworks / Zero Dependencies: Built without React, Vue, Webpack, Vite, Node runtime, or backend databases. 100% client-side execution.
  • Development & Version Control: Git version control hosted on GitHub, continuous automated deployment via Vercel, and automated cross-browser verification via Playwright.
  • AI Assistance: Code architecture and vector illustrations were developed with AI assistance (Google Antigravity), while the production application executes entirely client-side without any AI models, runtime tokens, or external API calls.

5. How the Project is Creative

  • Tactile Retro-Futuristic Mission Control Aesthetic: Inspired by classic mission control terminals and flight consoles, the interface uses high-contrast typography (Space Grotesk, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono), corner ticks, crisp status LEDs, segmented dials, and authentic hardware-styled consoles.
  • Procedural Vector Mission Patch Generator: Upon completing a mission, the game procedurally generates a customized, high-resolution mission insignia patch incorporating the spacecraft silhouette, destination target, flight grade, and crew callsign, which players can download as a digital keepsake.
  • Pass-the-Device Collaborative Dynamic: Rather than requiring multiplayer server infrastructure, Team Mode embraces the tactile social experience of a shared physical tablet or laptop. Secret priority briefings and a dedicated "Pass the Device" interstitial encourage real-world discussion and negotiation before the crew locks in their Flight Readiness Review.
  • Interactive Design Link Sharing: Designs serialize directly into URL query hash fragments, allowing players to share custom satellite configurations with friends or teachers via a simple link with zero server-side storage.

6. Factors Considered During Development

  • Educational Fidelity vs. Playful Simplicity: Real spacecraft engineering involves complex differential equations and multi-million-dollar budgets. We distilled these into an accessible, educational model informed by NASA public mission design guidelines (NASA Goddard Mission Design Lab, CubeSat 101, and NASA Science Mission concepts) while clearly disclosing that figures are illustrative and simplified for learning.
  • Universal Accessibility & Device Diversity: Every screen was engineered to adapt seamlessly from 360px mobile viewports up to 4K desktop displays, with fully accessible modal dialogs, keyboard navigation (Esc to close, focus trapping), high-contrast text ratios, and prefers-reduced-motion considerations.
  • Strict Privacy & Legal Hygiene: The application requires no logins, uses no cookies, collects no telemetry or analytics, and makes zero background network requests. All artwork and sound effects are original assets, strictly omitting copyrighted logos, trademarked insignia, or real mission telemetry to maintain complete legal and competition compliance.
